title: Ethiopian Red Lentil Stew
community: All of Ethiopia — the most important fasting dish in the cuisine
author: Mama Tigist

heritage.origin: All of Ethiopia — the fasting staple of the Orthodox Christian majority
heritage.history: Misir Wat is the most important vegetarian dish in Ethiopian cuisine — during the 200+ annual fasting days observed by Ethiopia's Orthodox Christian majority, when meat and dairy are prohibited, Misir Wat is the primary protein and the most beloved dish on the fasting table. Made from red lentils cooked in a berbere sauce built on dry-caramelised onions and oil (no kibbeh on fasting days), it is simultaneously the simplest and most satisfying of Ethiopian dishes. The key technique is identical to Key Wat: dry-caramelise the onions first, bloom the berbere in oil, then cook the lentils until they dissolve into the sauce.

desc: Ethiopian Misir Wat — red lentils cooked in a deeply spiced berbere sauce built on dry-caramelised onions and oil. The most important Ethiopian fasting dish — the lentils dissolve partially into the sauce, creating a thick, rich, intensely flavoured stew. Vegan, but extraordinary.
longDesc: Misir Wat is the proof that Ethiopian fasting food is not deprivation food — the berbere sauce built on 20 minutes of dry-caramelised onions produces a flavour depth that rivals the great meat wats. The red lentils dissolve partially, thickening the sauce naturally, and absorbing the berbere completely. Many Ethiopians and international visitors consider Misir Wat the single greatest Ethiopian dish.
ingredients: 4 tbsp vegetable oil (no kibbeh on fasting days)
steps: Dry caramelise onions — 20 minutes with no oil, stirring often.
Add oil. Stir to coat the caramelised onions.
Add berbere. Stir vigorously into the oil for 3—4 minutes — this is called 'frying the berbere'.
Add garlic, ginger, and tomato paste. Cook 2 minutes.
Add washed lentils. Stir to coat in the berbere sauce.
Add water. Bring to a boil.
Reduce heat. Simmer covered 30—35 minutes, stirring occasionally.
The lentils should partially dissolve — some whole, some dissolved into the sauce.
The sauce should be thick and deeply red.
chefTips: The dry-caramelised onion base is the absolute foundation — 20 minutes minimum.
Frying the berbere in oil is essential — it activates the fat-soluble colour and flavour compounds.
Red lentils dissolve much faster than green lentils — watch them from 25 minutes.
On fasting days: use oil, not kibbeh. On non-fasting days: kibbeh makes it richer.
commonMistakes: Not frying the berbere in oil first.
cookingScience: Red lentils have had their seed coat removed — this makes them absorb water and dissolve much faster than whole lentils. The dissolved lentil starch acts as a natural thickener. The berbere's carotenoids (fat-soluble) dissolve into the oil, creating the characteristic deep red colour — this only happens when the berbere is cooked in fat, not water.
sustainabilityTips: Lentils fix nitrogen in the soil — one of the most ecologically beneficial crops.
Very low water footprint compared to animal protein.
servedWith: On the fasting platter alongside Kik Alicha (ETH103)
storage: Refrigerate 5 days. Freeze 3 months. Improves overnight.
reheating: Gently with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Very high plant protein — 18g per cup cooked.
Very high in iron — critical during fasting periods when meat is avoided.
Prebiotic fibre from dissolved lentil starch.
culturalNote: Misir Wat is what Ethiopian fasting food is — the proof that vegetarian cooking can be as magnificent and deeply satisfying as any meat dish. During Lent, Ethiopian restaurants and homes serve Misir Wat on their fasting platters, and many international visitors discover it and understand immediately why Ethiopian cuisine is extraordinary. The combination of Misir Wat and injera is one of the world's great food pairings.
